The benchmark code is public (benchmarks/bench_protocol.cpp, which uses lemire/counters and a CMake default Release build), but the only platform detail for that table is 'Apple M4', with no compiler named, so the evidence stays at C.

corrections.caveats: No compiler is named for the headline billion-queries/s table (only 'Apple M4 processor'), and the table does not say whether it is the hits, misses or mixed workload. The bench builds as CMake Release by default, so it is capped at C. The committed perf_viz/baseline_results.json run (hardware and compiler unstated) shows a smaller gap for URL Protocols: hits 1.97 ns vs 13.32 ns for std::unordered_map (~6.8x); misses 3.33 vs 4.45 ns (~1.3x); mixed 5.75 vs 13.08 ns (~2.3x) (derived from page data). Other M3 Max figures in the README (wide container, ticker sets) compare only against absl::flat_hash_map and a trie, not std::unordered_map. Young project (repo created 2026-03-04, 17 stars), first-party numbers only, not independently reproduced.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C. hashtable-bench states the compilers (gcc 10.2.0 on the Threadripper 3990X under Ubuntu 20.04; clang 13.1.6 on the M1 Max under macOS 12.1) and the CPU models. Its README gives the build as CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, and CMakeLists.txt at the Jan-2022 data commit a6664ff adds -Wall -Wextra, plus -mcpu=native on Apple. The benchmark code is public (src/benchmark.cpp, src/maps/std_unordered_map/Map.h, src/seed-maps/dy_fph_map at 2bafe80), and it runs std::unordered_map directly against fph::DynamicFphMap, with per-size CSVs in results/data-3990x and results/m1-max.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Hit find() at max_load_factor 0.9 on uint64 split-bit-masked keys (hashtable-bench Figures 1-2 and CSVs). AMD 3990X: fph::DynamicFphMap+fph::SimpleSeedHash 2.04 ns vs std::unordered_map+std::hash 10.53 ns at n=32, and 30.98 vs 66.43 ns at n=10^7. That is 2.1-7.6x faster than the best std::unordered_map hash variant across n=32..10^7 (derived from page data). Apple M1 Max: 1.63 vs 2.43 ns (best std::unordered_map variant, robin_hood::hash) at n=32, and 14.79 vs 45.01 ns at n=10^7, i.e. 1.2-7.3x (derived from page data). std::unordered_map+std::hash (libc++) times out on this dataset above ~6000 elements on M1 Max. The fph-table README summarizes this only as a 'clear speed advantage'.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc 10.2.0 (AMD 3990X, Ubuntu 20.04) and clang 13.1.6 (M1 Max, macOS 12.1); CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (CMake default -O3 -DNDEBUG) with -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra, plus -mcpu=native on Apple (hashtable-bench CMakeLists.txt at data commit a6664ff, Jan 2022)
corrections.hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper 3990X (Zen2); Apple M1 Max (MacBook Pro 16-inch 2021)
corrections.workload: find() hits on uint64_t keys where only ceil(log2(n)) fixed split bit positions vary (hashtable-bench dataset 1), uint64_t values, map rehashed at max_load_factor 0.9, sizes 32 to 10^7; the time shown is the average time per operation over a throughput loop, compared across hash-table/hash-function pairs.
corrections.caveats: hashtable-bench is written by the fph-table author, so it is not independent (the tier does not depend on that). The README plots are a Jan-2022 snapshot. Current master added -march=native on Linux (2025) and moved the seeded fph maps to src/backup-seed-maps, so an exact reproduction needs the 2022 commit. The win depends on size and key distribution. On the 3990X, ska::flat_hash_map+std::hash beats fph below ~1000 elements, and absl::flat_hash_map wins large-n miss lookups. On M1 Max, std::unordered_map+std::hash (libc++) degenerates on this masked-bit dataset, so the fair baseline is the robin_hood::hash/absl::Hash variant. fph inserts are very slow (table rebuilds), so it only suits lookup-dominated or static key sets.

notes: Metadata matches: Apache-2.0, 55 stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-08-16. The record's claim that no compiler is stated was wrong, because the hashtable-bench README names both compilers. tier_reason: The README benchmark tables match the quoted numbers (string_view N=1024 map find: icy 3.228, std::map 44.393, std::unordered_map 5.278, tsl 4.595, sorted vector 23.987), and they run against std::map, std::unordered_map and std::set directly. The code is public (bench/bench_find.cpp) and the flags are in bench/CMakeLists.txt and the Makefile, but no compiler is stated (only 'M4 Max, 64 Go'), so the tier stays C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: std::string_view find() at N=1024: icy 3.228 'cycles/op' vs std::map 44.393, std::unordered_map 5.278, tsl::robin_map 4.595, sorted-vector+lb 23.987. Versus std::unordered_map/set the gain is 1.64-1.77x (map) and 1.69-1.72x (set) for string_view keys. For int64 keys it is only 1.02-1.25x (map) and 1.36-2.39x (set), and tsl::robin_set beats icy at int64 N=512. It is up to ~13.8x faster than std::map and ~14.9x faster than std::set (all ratios derived from page data). The README's own summary claims '1.5~2x' vs std::unordered_map/set 'with all optimizations enabled'.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Compiler not stated; bench/CMakeLists.txt forces -O3 -DNDEBUG -march=native on bench targets (overriding the -O level of the README's RelWithDebInfo config); the Makefile bench path uses cc -std=c++23 -O3 -march=native -fconstexpr-steps=4000000000
corrections.caveats: bench_find.cpp defines ICY_OPTIMIZE_KEY_CMP. With it, icy's string-key find() checks only the stored 64-bit hash and skips key equality, while the std containers do full key compares, so the string_view comparison is not like for like. All queries are hits; there is no miss workload. On aarch64 the timer is CNTVCT_EL0 (generic-timer ticks, not core cycles), so only the ratios are meaningful. No compiler is named. The README's CMake bench recipe is broken (bench/CMakeLists.txt adds a nonexistent bench.cpp, and there is no icy_bench target), so only the Makefile path builds. icy's near-zero iteration numbers come from a constexpr table and are plausibly constant-folded. Brand-new project (created 2026-09-11, 0 stars), author's own microbenchmark.
